I have several proposals, all of them start on this basis:

  1. We scratch Majority wins.
  2. META holds no value
  3. IRC holds no value
  4. Your action holds 1 vote in your favor

First proposal

Aye/Nay becomes a favorability % of the posts/curses/blessings. A post gets 5 Aye and 3 Nay => 66% chance it passes; 33% chance it doesn't.

This applies for each post/curse/blessing/... so it requires that players vote on the comments as well (if they feel inclined.)

second proposal

If there's a discussion breaking out, mods will ask for intent of the poster. No lawyer text wording allowed.

Third proposal

No creation of new elements in the comments. Comments are for interaction between existing pieces on the field or for cursing/blessing new pieces on the field. You cannot make use of any previously undefined instance to trump the other.

Fourth proposal

Interaction between races/heroes/demigods/gods has been awkward before.

If a any classes interact we need a modifier to their effect. Race vs race = 1/1 but race/god = 1/10 for example. if we can setup a powerscaling we can factor this into the dice rolls.

For example: Demigod (0.5) attacks a God (1).

Demigod gets 4 aye 2 nay on his attack of the god.

5 * 1 vs 2*2 makes the roll 5/9 to attack the god succesfully.

This is a really good idea, and I like the scaling. In the last game, gods were too powerful, and races lacked any sort of strength. An equaliser is a great idea.

I actually think that all these proposals will work well. :)

Another suggestion

Domains are the political goals of your god.

A god doing something inside his own domain gets a +1 baseline.

I'm a professional programmer. I sometimes joke that I actually don't know how to program, I just know how to Google for the code I need.

But in all honesty, data types aren't that difficult. It's much easier when you learn about how many bits or bytes of memory each data type takes up. A boolean takes up one bit, so its value can either be off or on, 0 or 1. A char takes up a byte (8 bits), so it can only have 2^8 different values. An integer is 4 bytes long, so it can hold up to 2^32 values. Signed variables use the first bit for the sign, so it can have values ranging from -2^(X-1) to +2^(X-1). The only different one is floating point, because of how the bits in a float are structured. All I care to know is that the range of a float is "enough for heavy computation".

For data types you'll learn them best by knowing what they're for, every one exists for a reason.

Learning syntax is a bit like learning a language, but it will only be confusing for the first language you learn. When you learn a second language it will seem intuitive.

So no, by the time you're experienced you'll know the syntax and data types easily (mostly you'll learn by actually using them). APIs are another matter, knowledge can be convenient since it saves googling but there's no way anyone can learn the APIs for any language, there's way too much. Everyone googles those.
I only have one for regex, because I almost never use it and then need reminders.

I remember everything I use regularly, like data types. And Google anything else I'm not 100% sure of. I've interviewed a lot and done a lot of interviewing. I am not a fan of whiteboard tests where you have to do everything from memory. I much prefer giving candidates practical programming problems to solve (similar to fizzbuzz) and let them use a real IDE and Google if they want. That's a much more realistic test of how they perform in a real world environment.

But be aware, when you are looking for a real job, you will probably get a lot of whiteboard tests and so you better know your shit.

You will always need to consult references or source code for one thing or another (syntax, APIs, limits, etc). When asked to recite the speed of sound, Albert Einstein allegedly said that he'd have to look it up--he didn't have room in his brain for trivia.

A better way forward than rote memorization is to skim over the details and then try to actually create something using what you've learned. Don't be afraid to do copious web searches along the way. I saw an article once that said the best programmers are the ones who reach for Google the soonest--and that makes sense to me.

Here are a couple particulars: 1) If you can, it'd be easier to learn C before C++since the latter is largely a superset of the former. 2) Regarding primitive types, the main things to know are a) that they can overflow b) they can be signed or unsigned c) starting at 8 bits they double in size 16, 32, 64 and you can plug 2^x into a calculator to get the limits.

You can also look them up if you think the range of values you're dealing with might overflow.
